themes.name: Own the verification loop
themes.claim_sentence: Trust in agent-generated systems comes from owning the verification loop—deterministic rules, stakes-scaled credentials, replayable execution traces, hardened sandboxes, and continuous failure diagnosis—rather than line-by-line diff review.
themes.definition: As generation drops to minutes, human diff review becomes the bottleneck and fails silently against compounding slop or benchmark gaming. Teams maintain quality at scale by converting corrections into code-enforced lint rules and invariants, gating tools by risk via Token Vault scopes and CIBA approvals, running agents in isolated VMs with video/trace artifacts, and closing an immune-system production loop that catches, diagnoses, remembers, and regression-tests failures—including cross-checking uncalibrated LLM judges in shadow mode.

themes.name: Brownfield & demand factories
themes.claim_sentence: Because coding tokens make small teams look huge on existing products with live runtime feedback, agentic software factories thrive on brownfield maintenance—bounded by real token/fuel economics and durable multi-hour execution.
themes.definition: When code generation is cheap, tiny pods (20–30 people, single high-equity units) ship and operate enterprise-scale products without traditional SaaS bloat or Jira ceremonies. However, greenfield 'open-ended discovery' factories amplify noise; factories excel on brownfield systems where customer telemetry and production SLAs define crisp promises to keep. Running long-horizon autonomous factories (and Demand Factories that extend the product envelope) is bounded less by code syntax than by compute fuel costs, sub-day sandbox durability across deploys, and steering multi-hour subagent loops.
also_called: every problem is a fuel problem

themes.name: Delete the harness
themes.claim_sentence: Stop over-engineering orchestration wrappers that models absorb every release; delete brittle scaffolding and invest in millisecond sandboxes, fast tool execution, semantic tool surfaces, and one shared organizational agent with public traces.
themes.definition: Prompt hacks, multi-step retrieval scaffolds, and tunnel-vision per-API wrappers degrade models and burn tokens as foundation models gain native bash/computer-use fluency. Teams achieve 3–4× speedups and fewer tokens by deleting 80–90% of harness glue each model generation while investing in durable infrastructure: instant-forking micro-VMs, edge low-latency runtimes where inference speed shifts bottlenecks to tool calls, and a single shared company agent whose public traces build institutional knowledge—though vertical domains still require workflow-specific harnesses encoded with expert taste.

themes.name: System One decision models
themes.claim_sentence: Sub-second, reliably calibrated decision models turn AI from heavy conversational chatbots into a programmatic fourth logic gate—running inside DuckDB queries, UI keystrokes, and live web-grounded pipelines.
themes.definition: Large frontier models are too slow and RLHF-sycophantic to use as inline software branching logic, and ungrounded LLMs suffer fatal overconfidence. Dedicated 'System One' decision models (Clef, Jev, TypeSafe, Grounded Decision Models backed by live 100B-page search indexes) deliver calibrated typed booleans, rankings, and citations under 1 second at roughly $1 per 1,000 requests—replacing entire embedding/vector-DB stacks and turning natural-language judgment into an ordinary composable function across SQL rows, search UIs, and routing boundaries.
themes.why_uncontested: Every speaker on decision models agrees on sub-second, typed, non-conversational invocation; talks diverge only on implementation surface (edge Edge Workers vs. DuckDB SQL functions vs. live web-index grounding) rather than contesting the architectural category.

themes.name: Modeled context over connectors
themes.claim_sentence: Wiring agents to dozens of live source connectors creates fragile chaos; reliable enterprise AI depends on unified permission-filtered indexes, warehouse data modeling, and actively pruned agent memory.
themes.definition: MCP solved plumbing, not answering: connecting an agent to live Slack, Jira, Drive, and operational databases leaves it guessing which source is canonical, violating ACLs, and drowning in contradictory context. High-leverage data and platform teams invest in the durable warehouse/semantic layer—building unified pre-computed search indexes with document-level ACL metadata attached at ingest—while curating agent memory through continuous scoring, consolidation ('dreaming'), and pruning so stale instructions do not poison future runs.

themes.name: Judgment when code is free
themes.claim_sentence: Zero-cost implementation shifts engineering value away from typing syntax toward human judgment, taste, ambition, and deliberate attention budgets—protecting teams from high-speed burnout.
themes.definition: Instant generation reverses 30 years of workflow economics: reviewing a 1,000-line PR takes just as much human cognition even when generating it costs $0. Builders must triage effort by 'expected pain' (probability of change × cost of changing later)—locking irreversible database schemas and interfaces carefully while keeping UI specs loose and visual. At the same time, compulsive multi-agent tabs trigger acute decision fatigue unless organizations shift away from ticket queues toward shared intent layers, extensible platforms, and bold ambition.

contested.question: Do the skills people built before AI carry over?

sides.stance: Coding skills fade with AI use, and much of what is lost no longer matters
The analytics skills data teams built are exactly what AI context needs

contested.question: Should a person stay in the loop on the decisions agents make?

sides.stance: Yes for uncertain cases: always-on agents queue them for a person to judge
No: a fast decision model lets the agent decide itself, without a human in the loop
Yes, at approval gates the team places wherever it wants them
Only until the model is reliable: an unpredictable miss is what forces a reviewer onto every answer
Yes for high stakes: approval on a separate channel (CIBA) before the tool runs
No: a thousand agents solved a 30-hour proof with no human steering on the solution
Yes at plan, design, and result level: automated checks alone leave generic output if humans bring no thinking
Yes: explore many directions rapidly, then pause to exercise human judgment past the first instant draft

contested.question: Should agent memory keep everything or be pruned?

sides.stance: Keep everything in an append-only log, and render the prompt from it per model
Prune on purpose: agents never delete, so memory becomes a garbage dump

contested.question: Should agents reach company data through each app or through one modeled store?

sides.stance: Through the modeled warehouse; a connection per source cannot join across sources
Through scoped access to each of the company's apps
Through MCP servers each domain owns, behind a shared platform that gates access and decides which source answers
Through one search index prepared ahead of time; one MCP server per source leaves the agent guessing

contested.question: Should agents search a prepared index or judge every row?

sides.stance: Index everything ahead of time into one search layer; it raised accuracy from about 40% to 97%
Skip the index: ask a decision model the question about every row directly

contested.question: Should developers work synchronously with coding agents or delegate asynchronously?

sides.stance: Synchronously with human-readable specs: asynchronous prompting breaks flow and leaves you ignorant of how the software behaves
Asynchronously over weeks: autonomous agents maintained Android/iOS parity for 44 days with almost no human messages
Continuously 24/7 in the background: brownfield factories should loop nonstop to keep existing customer promises
